title: States fume over Commonwealth's proposed private health insurance rebate changes
full_text:
The states and territories have set the stage for a showdown with the Commonwealth over its proposed private health insurance rebate changes, with some demanding the federal government ditch the plan amid new warnings it will worsen the strain on public hospitals.
Health ministers will head into a meeting this morning in Sydney armed with a list of concerns, including the Commonwealth's proposed changes to the private health insurance rebate for older Australians and the rapidly growing number of stranded aged care patients in public hospitals across the nation.
Currently, those aged 65 or over receive a larger rebate on premiums than someone aged under 65 on the same income.
However, earlier this year, the federal government announced it would seek to establish greater equity between generations by ditching the Howard-era policy, meaning more than 3 million older Australians would have to pay hundreds of dollars more for their private health insurance each year from next April.
The federal government's modelling has indicated that about 44,000 Australians would dump their private health insurance as a result.
Those figures have been backed by independent modelling from health economists at the University of Melbourne, who said the impact on hospitals would likely be small.
However, NSW Health Minister Ryan Park said his health department's modelling showed the proposed changes would have a much more significant impact on the public health system.
The upper end of the modelling estimates that in NSW alone, 80,000 residents aged 65 and over may either cancel or downgrade their private health insurance as a result.
It also estimates that it could result in public hospitals in NSW picking up more than 23,000 additional surgeries a year.
"The Commonwealth's proposed changes to private health insurance rebates will place additional pressure onto NSW's public hospitals at a time when health services are already experiencing significant demand," Mr Park said.
New South Wales is among states and territories like South Australia, Victoria and the Northern Territory which have raised concerns over the proposal.
"Any change that would leave older Victorians worse off and put additional pressure on Victoria's public hospitals is unacceptable," Victorian Health Minister Ingrid Stitt said.
However, the Queensland LNP and Tasmanian Liberal governments have gone further, demanding the plan be ditched.
"This is, I think, robbing Peter to pay Paul — and Paul hasn't been paid yet," Queensland Health Minister Tim Nicholls told the ABC.
"We think that the Commonwealth has not yet got a full understanding of the impact … if we see more people dropping out of private health insurance, then we'll see more people turning up in our public health institutions, including our public hospitals."
The issue has become increasingly political, with Shadow Health Minister Anne Ruston vowing the Coalition would block the legislation in the Senate because it was "nothing more than a cost shift onto older Australians to the public hospital system."
That means the federal government will need the support of the Greens to get the legislation through parliament, with the party yet to land on a formal position.
Despite the backlash, the federal government is vowing to push ahead with the plan, arguing the decision will save the government $3 billion over four years, with savings spent elsewhere in the aged care system.
"While some people may choose to leave private health insurance because of this change, we project this would be around 0.4 per cent," a government spokesperson said.
3,700 aged care patients stranded in public hospitals
The health ministers have also mobilised to launch another coordinated attack against the Commonwealth over the number of stranded aged care patients.
New figures collated by the states and territories have revealed there are now more than 3,700 aged care patients languishing in public hospitals across the country.
That is compared to about 2,500 last September, an increase of about 50 per cent in 12 months.
Those patients have been medically cleared for discharge but remain in hospital because there is nowhere suitable for them to go.
"I think it is the singular biggest issue that the South Australian health system faces today," South Australian Health Minister Blair Boyer told the ABC.
"They are beds that we don't have available to us today for people who might be presenting at an emergency department or arriving by ambulance, in some cases for elective surgery that is planned."
While states run public hospitals, the Commonwealth is responsible for funding and regulating aged care services.
Tensions flared in the lead-up to the latest public hospital funding agreement cinched in January, with state governments of different political stripes abandoning party allegiances to unite on the issue.
As well as occupying beds and placing increased pressure on hospitals, long stays in hospitals also strip elderly patients of independence and put them at a greater risk of illness and infection.
Tim Nicholls this week revealed a patient had been stranded in a Queensland public hospital for more than 1,000 days, with more than a dozen other patients stranded for more than 700 days.
He said long-stay patients accounted for more than 11 per cent of the state's acute hospital capacity.
"This is an enormous issue for all states," he said.
"Every bed that is taken up by someone who could be out of a hospital means that we can't move people out of our emergency departments and that means we can't transfer people from the back of an ambulance into an emergency department to receive treatment."
WA Health Minister Meredith Hammat said the issue had reached "worrying new heights".
"It is having an impact on people's ability to be able to access care in our hospitals where they've got acute care needs," she told the ABC.
The Commonwealth has pledged an additional 5,000 aged care beds a year by 2029 as part of a $3.7 billion package, alongside funding for specialist dementia care units and a joint taskforce examining long-stay hospital patients.
"Under the historic national hospital funding deal secured by the Albanese Labor Government in January, the Commonwealth is delivering an additional $24.4 billion in funding to the states and territories over 5 years to help them manage their hospital systems," a federal government spokesperson said.
"The Commonwealth expects that record $219.6 billion investment would flow into states and territories' hospital systems to help cut waiting lists, reduce waiting times in emergency rooms, and get older long-stay patients out of hospitals, and manage ramping."
